title: very slow scanning when there are many content-identical files
body: ### What happened? Since two or three releases ago (don't know exactly when this changed, but probably [v2.1.0](https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/releases/tag/v2.1.0)) scanning is terribly slow. In the past, scanning would take a few seconds (way less than a minute). Now on both my PC and laptop this process can take way over 10 minutes. At least one time, the laptop was scanning for hours. ### Syncthing version 2.1.1 ### Platform & operating system Linux x86-64 (Arch Linux) ### Browser version _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell Let me know what logs would be useful to debug this. ```

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I may be wrong here, but I wonder if this is related to the rename-tracking change from #10653.

Before that change, `findRename` added candidates to `alreadyUsedOrExisting` after checking them:

```go
alreadyUsedOrExisting[fi.Name] = struct{}{}

if !osutil.IsDeleted(f.mtimefs, fi.Name) {
    continue
}
```

So when many files had the same `BlocksHash`, a candidate that was already checked and still existed would normally be skipped the next time.

The current code seems to remember only files that were already used as rename sources:

```go
if batch.hasDeleted(fi.Name) {
    continue
}

if !osutil.IsDeleted(f.mtimefs, fi.Name) {
    continue
}
```

Could this mean that for every changed file, Syncthing goes through the same content-identical candidates again and repeats the `IsDeleted` checks?

With lots of identical small files, such as files inside multiple `.git` directories, this could become roughly:

```text
changed files × files with the same BlocksHash
```

That would seem consistent with the scan spending most of its time looking for possible renames.

Maybe the candidates could be cached per `BlocksHash` for the current batch. On the first lookup, Syncthing could check all matching files once and remember only the deleted candidates, or remember that there are none. Used candidates could then be removed from that cache, and the whole cache could be cleared when the batch is flushed.

This should hopefully keep the reduced memory usage from #10653 while avoiding repeated database iteration and filesystem checks for the same group of identical files.

I have not tested or benchmarked this, so this is just a possible explanation based on comparing the old and current `findRename` code.

I did some further verification of the hypothesis above, with Codex helping me inspect the history, analyze the attached profile, and build a small regression test.

An automated `git bisect` between v2.0.16 and v2.1.0 identified [`[2721b7b5](https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/commit/2721b7b5222ff414d02b35789a82028508918a8e)`](https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/commit/2721b7b5222ff414d02b35789a82028508918a8e) - #10653 as the first bad commit.

In a controlled test with 400 content-identical files, after changing every mtime and rescanning:

* immediately before #10653: 799 `Lstat` calls, about 405 ms;
* after #10653 - current behavior: 160,000 `Lstat` calls, about 1 second.

The call counts match the suspected behavior exactly: previously this was 400 scanner stats plus 399 rename-candidate checks; now it is 400 scanner stats plus 400 × 399 repeated candidate checks. The elapsed times are only from a local test, but the call counts are deterministic.

The CPU profile from the second support bundle points to the same path: `findRename` accounts for 85.1% of sampled CPU and `osutil.IsDeleted` for 78.9%.

There is also a strong historical clue: #7315, merged in 2021, explicitly introduced `alreadyUsedOrExisting` to fix slow scans where newly scanned data contained many duplicates, by caching candidates already checked with `IsDeleted`. It looks like #10653 removed that optimization while fixing the separate memory-growth problem.

With Codex's help, I also tried a small per-`BlocksHash`, per-batch cache matching the idea above. It reduced the test from 160,000 to 800 `Lstat` calls and from about 1 second to about 72 ms, and `go test ./lib/model` still passed. This is only a local prototype, not a production-ready patch, but it seems to validate the general direction.

I don't know Go particularly well; my main languages are Bash and Python. This issue caught my attention because I was planning to use Syncthing for a similar use case, so I had a personal reason to investigate it. Hopefully someone familiar with the codebase can turn this into a proper patch. If nobody picks it up, I can try to work on one with Codex assisting me.

comments.body:
@reporter I tried it with your repo. Good suggestion, because it makes the difference much easier to see.

I compared the commit immediately before #10653 (`b1ccf3f3`) with the #10653 commit itself (`2721b7b5`).

A fresh clone of the repo was not particularly slow:

| Test | Before #10653 | After #10653 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rescan fresh clone | 0.21 s / 1,989 `Lstat` calls | 0.35 s / 3,190 `Lstat` calls |

However, a fresh clone does not contain `.git/subtree-cache`, because that is locally generated Git data. Your logs showed many files under `.git/subtree-cache/.../notree`, so I tried to reproduce that part as well.

I ran `git subtree split --prefix=nist-sts`, which generated 1,973 cache files. There were two particularly large groups of content-identical files:

- 1,378 identical 41-byte files
- 594 identical 2-byte `notree` files

I then indexed the plain clone, added this generated subtree cache and scanned again:

| Test | Before #10653 | After #10653 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Scan 1,973 newly added cache files | 2.50 s / 15,559 `Lstat` calls | 22.71 s / 1,585,647 `Lstat` calls |

I repeated this test twice with fresh copies. The times were:

- before: 2.46 s and 2.54 s
- after: 23.05 s and 22.37 s

The `Lstat` counts were exactly the same in both runs. So after #10653 this particular scan made about 102 times more `Lstat` calls and took about 9 times longer.

I also tried a heavier rescan by changing the mtimes of all 2,369 files:

| Test | Before #10653 | After #10653 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rescan cache-heavy clone | 9.54 s / 22,908 `Lstat` calls | 131.46 s / 9,366,876 `Lstat` calls |

That is about 409 times more `Lstat` calls and almost 14 times longer.

These are local timings, so the absolute numbers will depend on the machine and filesystem. I think the call counts are more useful here, especially because they were repeatable.

I measured only scanning rather than an actual transfer, since the profile showed that the time was being spent in `findRename` and `IsDeleted` before synchronization.

One caveat is that these exact historical revisions predate the configurable `blockIndexing` option, so I could not disable it for this A/B test. It should not affect the comparison between the two adjacent commits, though.

So yes, this seems to confirm that the regression is real. The plain PKGBUILDs clone shows only a small difference, but its locally generated `.git/subtree-cache` makes the problem much worse. That also seems to explain why ignoring `.git` was such an effective workaround for you.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
@reporter I went back to this after your v2.1.3 report and ran a broader set of
isolated benchmarks. I need to qualify what I said earlier: #10833 fixes the
repeated `IsDeleted` problem I measured in the 400+400-file test, but it does
not completely restore the pre-regression behavior once a scan crosses an
update-batch boundary. There is also a separate database iteration cost which
#10833 does not address.

I tested `b1ccf3f3` (before #10653), `2721b7b5` (first bad), `ec35a953`
(#10819), `ed6b56d4` (#10833), `946e2b83` (v2.1.3), and current `main` at
`328d910aee822178f55442c76bc7e35ce34d68cc`. Each repetition used a fresh
home, database, and test directory. The watcher and periodic rescans were off,
and only the manual scan was timed. These are medians of three runs after a
separate correctness run, with a 120 s timeout:

| Test | Before #10653 | First bad | With relevant fix | v2.1.3 | `main` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Add 400 identical files to 400 existing files | 0.543 s | 11.569 s | #10833: 0.423 s | 0.443 s | 0.423 s |
| Add 2,000 identical files to 2,000 existing files | 12.131 s | >120 s | #10833: 9.253 s | 9.304 s | 9.240 s |
| Fresh database with 4,000 identical files | 14.635 s | >120 s | #10833: 11.093 s | 11.191 s | 11.190 s |
| Change only mtimes of 2,000 identical existing files | 9.837 s | >120 s | #10819: 0.584 s | 0.686 s | 0.626 s |
| Rewrite 2,000 existing files to identical content | 2.877 s | 25.061 s | #10819: 0.503 s | 0.584 s | 0.524 s |

The timings are specific to my machine. The more useful result came from
counting candidate rows returned by `AllLocalFilesWithBlocksHash` and
`IsDeleted` calls made by `findRename`.

In the 400+400 test the first bad commit returned 160,000 candidate rows and
made 160,000 `IsDeleted` calls. With #10833 it still returned all 160,000 rows,
but made only 400 `IsDeleted` calls. So the original result was real: #10833
does fix the repeated filesystem checks within one batch.

Across several batches I got this instead:

| Test | Revision | Candidate rows | `IsDeleted` calls |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Add 2,000 to 2,000 | before #10653 | 5,000,999 | 3,999 |
| Add 2,000 to 2,000 | #10833 / v2.1.3 / `main` | 5,000,999 | 8,998 |
| Fresh 4,000 | before #10653 | 6,006,951 | 3,993 |
| Fresh 4,000 | #10833 / v2.1.3 / `main` | 6,006,951 | 9,972 |

The check counts follow the 1,000-file flushes exactly. For a fresh scan on
v2.1.3 they were:

```text
1,000 files:    993
2,000 files:  2,986 = 993 + 1,993
4,000 files:  9,972 = 993 + 1,993 + 2,993 + 3,993
```

This seems to come from `clear(b.skipInFindRename)` in the batch callback. The
old `alreadyUsedOrExisting` map lasted for the whole scan; the new map lasts
for one `scanBatch`. A candidate confirmed to exist is therefore remembered
inside a batch and checked again after the next flush. I also checked the batch
code with a small Go test: the same callback runs at exactly 1,000 files or
5,000 blocks. The file boundary is visible above; I only checked the block
boundary at Go level.

The other remaining part is candidate iteration. Here is the fresh-database
scaling result for v2.1.3:

| Files | Scan time | Candidate rows | Rows/file |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 500 | 0.141 s | 0 | 0 |
| 1,000 | 0.384 s | 6,951 | 6.951 |
| 2,000 | 2.316 s | 1,006,951 | 503.476 |
| 4,000 | 11.237 s | 6,006,951 | 1,501.738 |

Going from 2,000 to 4,000 files increased the row count 5.97x and scan time
4.85x. `findRename` still performs one lookup for every new nonempty file, and
matching rows are yielded before `skipInFindRename` is consulted. #10833 saves
filesystem calls after those rows have been decoded; it does not save the
queries or row decoding. As a control, 3,000 same-sized files with unique
contents produced 3,000 lookups, zero candidate rows, and zero rename-related
`IsDeleted` calls. Toggling block indexing did not change these counts.

#10819 is clearer. In both existing-path cases above (mtime-only changes and
content rewrites), rename lookups, candidate rows, and `IsDeleted` calls all
went to zero. It cannot help the fresh-database case because there is no old
entry for the path to compare with.

All completed correctness runs ended with the expected paths and hashes. Four
first-bad runs hit the timeout and were stopped. The first-bad profile for the
2,000+2,000 test had about 75% of cumulative sampled CPU below
`osutil.IsDeleted` and about 73% below the `Lstat` stack, which agrees with the
old failure mode. After #10833, the exact 4,000-file counts (6,006,951 database
rows versus 9,972 checks) point to database iteration as the larger remaining
avoidable cost in this synthetic case.

v2.1.3 therefore matches the pre-regression behavior for the single-batch B1
case, and #10819 removes the regression path in B4/B5. It does not match the
old filesystem-check counts for multi-batch B2/B3, even though it happened to
finish faster on this machine. The candidate-row counts in B2/B3 are the same
as before the regression. Current `main` has no later change in this code and
gave the same counters as v2.1.3.

This also makes your v2.1.3 result plausible without contradicting the earlier
400+400 benchmark. The worst per-row filesystem checking is gone, but a fresh
database still hashes every file, and a large identical-content group can
still cause millions of SQLite candidate rows to be read. Without a profile
from the slow real-world scan I cannot say which one dominates there.

For a regression test, I think the smallest useful case would use an injectable
batch limit (say 8) and 17-24 identical nonempty files with counted fake
database and filesystem operations. It should check that a confirmed-existing
candidate is tested at most once per scan, including across flushes, and that
the same candidate rows are not decoded once per file. A separate test at the
real 1,000-file boundary would make sense too.

For a fix, I would first separate batch-local “rename source already consumed”
state from scan-wide “candidate confirmed to exist” state. Caching candidates
by `(BlocksHash, size)` for the duration of the scan would address the repeated
database iteration as well.
